title: SHE TOUCHED HIS ROBE, BUT HE TOUCHED HER IDENTITY: WHY JESUS CALLED A BLEEDING WOMAN “DAUGHTER”
paragraphs: SHE TOUCHED HIS ROBE, BUT HE TOUCHED HER IDENTITY: WHY JESUS CALLED A BLEEDING WOMAN “DAUGHTER”
For twelve years, her body had been bleeding. In one encounter, Jesus gave her something even deeper than physical healing—and perhaps it is exactly what your wounded soul has been searching for.
Imagine suffering for so long that you can barely remember who you were before the pain began.
Imagine waking up every morning hoping something would change, only to discover that yesterday's suffering had followed you into another day.
You prayed.
You waited.
You exhausted your resources.
You watched other people receive the very things you had been begging God for.
And somewhere between your unanswered questions and your silent tears, you began wondering whether God still saw you.
Whether He still cared.
Whether you still belonged.
There was a woman in Scripture who understood that kind of suffering.
We do not know her name. We do not know what her voice sounded like, what dreams she once carried, or how many nights she cried herself to sleep.
But we know what had happened to her.
And more importantly, we know what Jesus called her.
Daughter.
One word.
Two thousand years later, that word still carries enough tenderness to confront the shame of a wounded soul.
Mark 5:25–26 tells us:
“And a certain woman, which had an issue of blood twelve years, and had suffered many things of many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse.”
Twelve years.
Approximately 4,383 days of living with a condition she could not overcome.
This was not simply an inconvenience. It was a prolonged physical affliction with financial, religious, and potentially devastating social consequences.
According to Leviticus 15:25–27, a woman experiencing an abnormal discharge of blood was considered ceremonially unclean for the duration of that discharge.
The Hebrew word associated with this condition is טָמֵא — tamé, meaning ritually or ceremonially unclean.
But we must understand something important.
Ceremonial uncleanness was not automatically evidence of personal sin, moral corruption, or divine punishment.
This woman was suffering from a bodily condition. Scripture does not accuse her of wickedness.
Yet the requirements surrounding ritual purity could profoundly affect ordinary human contact, religious participation, and daily life.
Imagine having to navigate those restrictions for twelve years.
Imagine the exhaustion of constantly being aware of your condition.
Imagine the possibility of people becoming more conscious of what was happening to your body than of what was happening inside your heart.
The Bible does not tell us precisely how her community treated her. But the burden described in the text is already heartbreaking enough without inventing details.
She had spent everything.
She had endured many treatments.
And instead of recovering, she had grown worse.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
Not necessarily because you have the same illness, but because you have been fighting something that seems determined to outlast you.
A marriage that is falling apart.
A sickness that keeps returning.
An addiction you are ashamed to admit.
A financial crisis that has swallowed your peace.
A childhood wound that still influences your adult relationships.
A private battle with sin that nobody knows about.
A depression that makes even getting out of bed feel like an achievement.
You have become skilled at smiling while suffering.
You tell people you are fine because explaining what is happening inside you feels more exhausting than pretending.
And sometimes the most painful part is not the suffering itself.
It is the fear that suffering has become your identity.
But then, this woman heard about Jesus.
Mark 5:27–28 says:
“When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment. For she said, If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole.”
She did not have an impressive introduction.
She did not arrive with wealth, influence, or religious credentials.
She came through the crowd carrying twelve years of suffering and a desperate confidence that Jesus could do what no one else had been able to do.
She reached for His garment.
And immediately, something happened.
Mark 5:29 records that the flow of blood stopped, and she knew in her body that she had been healed of her affliction.
She had come seeking healing.
She could have disappeared into the crowd.
But Jesus stopped.
“Who touched my clothes?” — Mark 5:30
The disciples were bewildered. People were pressing against Him from every direction.
Yet Jesus continued looking around.
The woman, frightened and trembling, came forward, fell before Him, and told Him the whole truth.
The whole truth.
Not a carefully edited testimony.
Not a version designed to protect her reputation.
Not merely the beautiful ending.
She told Him the truth.
There is something deeply moving about that moment.
For twelve years, her condition had shaped her life. Now she was standing before the One who had the authority to heal her.
And what would He say?
Would He rebuke her?
Would He embarrass her?
Would He treat her as an interruption?
Jesus was already on His way to the house of Jairus, whose daughter was desperately ill.
There was another emergency waiting.
Another family crying.
Another life in danger.
Yet Jesus made room for this suffering woman.
He did not treat her as an inconvenience.
And then He spoke the words that have echoed through generations.
“Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague.” — Mark 5:34
The original Greek reads:
Θυγάτηρ, ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε· ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην, καὶ ἴσθι ὑγιὴς ἀπὸ τῆς μάστιγός σου.
Thygatēr, hē pistis sou sesōken se; hypage eis eirēnēn, kai isthi hygiēs apo tēs mastigos sou.
A close English rendering is:
“Daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace, and be healthy, free from your affliction.”
The first word is extraordinary.
Θυγάτηρ — Thygatēr.
Daughter.
A word of familial relationship, used here as a tender and reassuring form of address.
In the recorded Gospel accounts, this is the only individual woman whom Jesus directly addresses with this particular word.
He could have simply confirmed her healing.
He could have told her that she was free to leave.
Instead, He addressed her with tenderness before sending her away in peace.
The woman who had approached Him trembling was not dismissed as a stranger who had inconvenienced Him.
She was called daughter.
Jesus did not merely acknowledge what had happened to her body.
His words communicated personal care, dignity, and reassurance.
And perhaps that is where this story begins to reach into the deepest places of our own lives.
Because sometimes, what we need most is not merely for something painful to stop.
We need to know that we are still loved while we are hurting.
We need to know that our worst experiences have not made us invisible to God.
We need to know that our wounds do not have the final authority to determine who we are.
Perhaps someone abandoned you and made you feel unwanted.
Perhaps your own failures have made you believe you are beyond forgiveness.
Perhaps people remember your scandal more clearly than they remember your humanity.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to prove that you deserve to be loved.
But the Gospel is not the story of human beings earning their way into God's family.
It is the story of Jesus Christ making redemption possible for people who could never save themselves.
John 1:12 declares:
“But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name.”
Through faith in Christ, believers receive the privilege of becoming children of God.
Romans 8:15 speaks of the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba, Father.”
The Aramaic word אַבָּא — Abba means Father, expressing a genuine familial relationship of trust and belonging.
The Gospel does not merely offer a better public image.
It offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a new identity in Christ.
That is why your past does not have to become your permanent address.
But notice something else in Jesus' words to the woman.
Σέσωκέν σε — Sesōken se.
This expression comes from the Greek verb σῴζω — sōzō, which can mean to save, rescue, deliver, or heal, depending on the context.
Here, the immediate context clearly includes physical healing. The perfect-tense form also presents the saving or healing action as accomplished, with a resulting state.
Jesus was confirming what had happened to her.
However, we must not misunderstand His statement about faith.
Her faith was not a magical force.
The fabric of His garment was not a supernatural formula.
She was not healed because she had mastered a spiritual technique.
Her faith was directed toward Jesus.
The power belonged to Christ, not to the woman.
And that distinction matters because there are wounded believers who have been made to feel guilty for remaining sick.
They have been told that if they possessed enough faith, their cancer would disappear.
If they prayed correctly, their depression would end.
If they believed harder, their disability would vanish.
But Scripture does not give us permission to make those promises.
Paul experienced an affliction that God did not remove despite repeated prayer (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).
Timothy experienced recurring physical ailments (1 Timothy 5:23).
Trophimus was left sick at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20).
Faithfulness to Christ does not guarantee immediate physical healing in this present life.
God can heal miraculously. He can also work through medicine, treatment, counseling, and the care of others. And sometimes, His sustaining grace meets us in suffering that remains.
The ultimate promise of complete restoration belongs to the resurrection and the coming renewal of all things (Revelation 21:4).
So please hear this.
If you are still suffering, your suffering is not automatic proof that your faith is defective.
If your prayers have not been answered in the way you hoped, that does not mean Jesus has stopped caring.
You can belong to Christ while your body is still weak.
You can trust Him while your eyes are still filled with tears.
You can be deeply loved by God while walking through circumstances you do not understand.
You do not owe the internet the private details of your pain. But perhaps those words can become a simple prayer and an encouragement to someone else who feels alone.
There is another remarkable detail hidden in the structure of Mark's account.
The suffering woman had been bleeding for twelve years.
Jairus's daughter was twelve years old.
For as long as one girl had been alive, another woman had been suffering.
One was identified through the name and position of her father, a synagogue leader.
The other remains unnamed in Scripture.
Yet Jesus showed compassion to both.
Mark places their stories together in Mark 5:21–43, inviting us to witness Christ's authority over disease and death.
While Jesus was speaking to the woman, news arrived that Jairus's daughter had died.
But Jesus was not defeated by the apparent delay.
He went to the house, took the girl by the hand, and spoke words that Mark preserves in Aramaic:
Ταλιθὰ κούμ — Talitha koum.
“Little girl, I say to you, arise.” — Mark 5:41
And she rose.
Consider the beauty of these intertwined encounters.
A suffering woman reaches out and touches Jesus.
Jesus reaches out and takes the hand of a dead child.
Under the ceremonial laws of the Old Testament, abnormal bodily discharges and contact with the dead were associated with ritual uncleanness (Leviticus 15:25–27; Numbers 19:11).
Yet in these encounters, suffering and death do not overcome Jesus.
His healing authority overcomes them.
The woman is healed.
The child is raised.
The One standing before them is not merely another religious teacher offering comforting words.
He is the Lord who possesses authority over what humanity cannot conquer.
And this points us toward something greater.
The cross.
Because the same Jesus who stopped for a bleeding woman would eventually shed His own blood.
The same Jesus who spoke peace to a trembling sufferer would endure the agony of crucifixion.
The same Jesus who restored a little girl to life would Himself enter death and rise victorious on the third day.
He did not come merely to improve our circumstances.
He came to save sinners.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
Christ bore our sins so that through Him we might be reconciled to God.
First Peter 2:24 connects His wounds with our deliverance from sin and our calling to live in righteousness.
The deepest human problem is not simply that we suffer.
It is that sin has separated us from God.
And the greatest miracle is not merely that a bleeding body can be healed.
It is that a guilty sinner can be forgiven, a rebellious heart can be transformed, and a person spiritually dead in sin can receive new life through Jesus Christ.
That is grace.
Grace does not pretend that sin is harmless.
Grace does not erase our responsibility to repent.
Grace does not give us permission to return comfortably to the very things from which Christ calls us to turn.
Grace meets us in the truth of our condition and offers what we could never purchase for ourselves.
Forgiveness.
Redemption.
Reconciliation.
New life.
The woman had spent everything she possessed seeking relief from her condition.
But the mercy she received from Jesus was not something she purchased.
And neither is your salvation.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9
You cannot buy your way into God's family.
You cannot donate your way into forgiveness.
You cannot earn eternal life through religious activity.
You come to Christ through repentance and faith, trusting in what He has accomplished through His death and resurrection.
And when you truly understand the grace you have received, generosity becomes a response to love rather than an attempt to purchase it.
Now return for a moment to that woman standing before Jesus.
Her body had been healed.
She had told Him the whole truth.
And He said:
“Go in peace.”
The Greek expression is ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην — hypage eis eirēnēn, literally, “go into peace.”
The word εἰρήνη — eirēnē means peace and carries rich biblical associations with the Hebrew concept of שָׁלוֹם — shalom, which encompasses peace, well-being, and wholeness.
Jesus sent her away with reassurance rather than condemnation.
She did not have to leave trembling in fear of His response.
And perhaps you have spent too many years trembling before an image of God that you constructed out of human rejection.
You think He must be as impatient as the people who abandoned you.
As unforgiving as the people who constantly remind you of your past.
As disappointed as the voices that tell you that you will never change.
But look at Jesus.
Look at how He receives this frightened woman.
Look at how He makes time for her.
Look at how He speaks.
The holiness of Christ does not make Him indifferent to human suffering.
His compassion does not make Him indifferent to sin.
In Him, perfect holiness and perfect mercy meet.
You do not need to pretend before Him.
You do not need to conceal the things He already knows.
Bring Him your grief.
Confess your sin.
Bring Him your questions.
Bring Him the broken pieces of the life you thought you had ruined beyond repair.
Hebrews 4:16 invites us to approach the throne of grace with confidence, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
And remember, the purpose of coming to Jesus is not merely to receive something from His hands.
It is to receive Him.
To know Him.
To follow Him.
To surrender to Him.
To discover that even when your circumstances remain difficult, Christ Himself is a treasure that suffering cannot take away.
Maybe you arrived at this article looking for an explanation of a single word in Scripture.
But perhaps that word has confronted something much deeper inside you.
You have been calling yourself a failure.
A disappointment.
A lost cause.
A burden.
Someone too damaged to be useful.
Someone too sinful to be forgiven.
Yet the authority to define your identity does not belong to your shame.
For those who are in Christ, Scripture declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1
That does not mean there are no consequences for our actions.
It means condemnation no longer has the final word over those who belong to Christ.
There is room for repentance.
There is hope for transformation.
There is mercy for the person who returns to God.
Your scandal may explain where you have been, but it does not have the authority to determine where the grace of Jesus can take you.
We want to create a place where biblical truth is not diluted, repentance is not avoided, grace is not cheapened, and wounded people are continually pointed toward Jesus Christ.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), while also reminding us that giving must come willingly from the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
It is an opportunity to participate in sustaining a ministry committed to pointing people toward Christ.
If you believe in what we are building and are able to help, we would be grateful to have you walk alongside us as a monthly supporter.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
Grace is not for sale.
Jesus remains the center of everything we do.
Before you leave, remember that unnamed woman.
She approached Jesus from behind, carrying twelve years of suffering.
She reached for His garment.
She fell before Him trembling.
She told Him the whole truth.
And the Savior who knew her condition did not reduce her to it.
He called her daughter.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that if people knew the whole truth about you, they would walk away.
But Jesus already knows.
He knows the sins that need forgiving.
The wounds that need tending.
The pride that needs surrendering.
The tears that nobody has witnessed.
The parts of your story that you wish you could erase.
And still, He calls sinners to repentance, invites the weary to come to Him, and promises never to cast out those who come to Him in faith (Matthew 11:28; John 6:37).
Do not let shame keep you hiding from the One who alone can redeem you.
Come to Jesus.
Not because you have finally become worthy.
But because He is merciful.
Not because you have successfully rewritten your past.
But because through His cross and resurrection, He offers a future that your past could never purchase.
The world may remember what happened to you.
People may remember what you did.
But in Christ, neither suffering nor forgiven sin gets to write the final chapter.

She came hoping Jesus would stop her bleeding. She left knowing that the One who held authority over her suffering had not forgotten her humanity. And the voice that called her daughter was louder than twelve years of pain.
